presenceLabel: Tutelo village or refuge in this area
presenceNote: First documented: Totero Town near Salem, Virginia, in September 1671 (Batts and Fallam); last documented homeland period: Coreorgonel, Tompkins County, New York, under Cayuga protection until the Sullivan Expedition of 1779. ‘Totteroy’ is a name that appears for the Big Sandy River on British maps of 1755–76. Griffin (1942) found no historic evidence that the Tutelo ever lived on that stream, and calls the name a map label, so nothing is drawn in Kentucky or on the Big Sandy. Low–medium confidence.
overlapNote: Saponi, Occaneechi, Monacan and Manahoac in the Virginia Piedmont; Susquehannock refugees camped near the Occaneechi in 1676; Catawba; Oneida (Shikellamy at Shamokin), Cayuga (the adoption of 1753) and Tuscarora. The Kentucky ‘Totteroy’ name is a map label only.
basis: Colonial records (Batts and Fallam 1671, Lawson 1701), archaeology at the Graham-White site in Salem, and Haudenosaunee records, via Wikipedia, Virginia Places, Access Genealogy and Griffin 1942. Mostly tertiary web sources.

eras.label: 1671–1701 · Roanoke valley, Virginia
eras.text: In September 1671 Batts and Fallam were ‘exceedingly civilly entertain’d’ at Totero Town, probably the Graham-White site at Salem (Virginia Places; the site is disputed). A few years later the Tutelo joined the Saponi on islands in the Roanoke River above the Occaneechi, near Clarksville (Wikipedia; Virginia Places). After Bacon’s Rebellion (1676) many moved toward the Yadkin, and in 1701 Lawson found them on the headwaters of the Yadkin in North Carolina (not drawn: the counties are not named). The tint is Roanoke County, the city of Salem and Mecklenburg County, Virginia: a general area.

eras.label: 1714–1730s · Fort Christanna, Brunswick County, Virginia
eras.text: Governor Spotswood built Fort Christanna on the Meherrin River, Brunswick County, in 1714–15 and gathered about 300 Saponi, Tutelo, Occaneechi and others; the 1714 treaty names the Tottero (Virginia Places). The fort was ordered abandoned in 1718 and was empty by 1722, but the Indian town stayed nearby. By 1740 most had been forced to leave their homeland for the north (Wikipedia); the tint ends here in the 1730s, where the next area begins.

eras.label: 1730s–1753 · Shamokin, Pennsylvania
eras.text: In the 1730s Tutelo people moved north to Shamokin (modern Sunbury, Pennsylvania) and sought the protection of the Oneida viceroy Shikellamy, whose wife was Tutelo (Wikipedia). This rests on one source, and the slider’s 1735 is a round number standing for ‘the 1730s’.

eras.label: 1753–1779 · Coreorgonel, near Ithaca, New York
eras.text: In 1753 the Cayuga formally adopted the Tutelo and Saponi, who settled at the south end of Cayuga Lake at Coreorgonel, near Ithaca (Wikipedia; Access Genealogy). The Sullivan Expedition destroyed the village in 1779, and the Tutelo went with the Cayuga to Canada, to what became the Six Nations of the Grand River. The last known fluent speaker died in 1898. The tint is Tompkins County, a general area; the Cayuga and the Six Nations also lived in the same country.
